analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover newborns for 30 days after birth, even before parents enroll them.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 30, 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship, was sent to three House committees and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a newborn is usually covered by a parent's health plan only after the parent adds the baby to the policy. Babies who need intensive care in their first weeks — before the paperwork is done — can leave parents with enormous bills. This bill would require every health plan to automatically cover a newborn for 30 days after birth, whether or not the baby has been enrolled, give parents a 60-day window afterward to add the baby, and require the plan to notify parents immediately if a claim comes in for a baby who is not yet enrolled. It applies to job-based plans, individual market plans, and self-insured employer plans.
analysis.who_benefits: New parents — especially mothers of babies who land in the neonatal intensive care unit in their first weeks of life, when a stay can cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. Under the bill, the plan must pay those claims even if the baby was not yet added to the policy, and parents get a protected window to enroll the baby afterward without fear of a surprise bill.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans, insurers, and self-insured employer plans to cover a newborn for the 30 days after birth for any service the plan otherwise covers, regardless of whether the baby has been enrolled [S2].
Creates a special enrollment period of at least 60 days after those 30 days for parents to add the newborn to the plan [S2].
Requires plans that receive a claim for an unenrolled newborn to immediately notify the parent that the baby is not enrolled, so the problem can be fixed instead of surfacing as a denied claim [S2].
Amends the same protections into the three statutes that govern employer plans, individual and group insurance, and tax-preferred health coverage, so no major type of coverage is left out [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor health plans bear the cost of paying claims for newborns who were not yet enrolled, which may feed into premiums. Insurers partially offset this by gaining new paying enrollees through the 60-day enrollment window.

drawbacks.text: Covering unenrolled newborns is a new obligation for plans and insurers, and those costs would ultimately be spread across premiums paid by all enrollees [S2].
The automatic coverage lasts only 30 days; parents who miss the following 60-day enrollment window would again be responsible for the baby's care costs after that [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection addresses a narrow but catastrophic risk: a NICU stay for a newborn who was never added to a plan can cost a family six figures. The cost to insurers and premiums is real but proportionally small, and the enrollment window encourages families to add babies promptly. The design is narrow enough that its main weakness is what it does not do — protection ends after 30 days.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means — none of which has taken it up, and it has no vote scheduled [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on July 30, 2026, joined by Reps. Ashley Hinson, Nanette Barragan, and Brian Fitzpatrick [S2].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means Committees [S4].
The bill has 3 cosponsors — 2 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S3].
No committee has held a hearing or markup and no vote has occurred since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: health insurers do not yet bear the cost of covering unenrolled newborns, and families of babies needing early intensive care remain exposed to the bills the bill would prevent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers; families still face the risk

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require 30-day automatic newborn coverage [S2][S4].

for.name: Rep. Ashley Hinson
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction [S2][S3].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan from the start — one Democrat plus two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors — and no opposition has yet appeared in the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans must pay claims for newborns who were never enrolled, a new cost, but the 60-day enrollment window turns those families into paying enrollees. The industry's interest runs alongside families' here: the bill shifts a rare catastrophic cost away from parents.

analysis.trajectory: Referral to three committees makes scheduling harder, since any one chair would need to act. Most House bills die in committee without a vote, and with no markup, hearing, or movement in the month since introduction, the odds of floor action before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 look poor unless a committee chair takes it up or it is attached to a larger health package.
